new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexically contrastive and not predictable; it may fall on the final syllable (open or closed), an open penult, or an open antepenult, but not on a closed penult or closed antepenult. A stressed open penult is phonetically lengthened. Certain suffixes and enclitics (PV -en, specificity =i, enclitic pronouns, perfective <in>, stative me-) shift stress one syllable rightward.
new_statements.secondary_stress: When an enclitic pronoun attracts primary stress to the new ultima, secondary stress may remain on the original stressed syllable (now antepenult), with lengthening and lowering of /i/ (sec. 3.2.7.3.2, ex. 3.41 [mənlaˌtɪ:=ʔa'mi]).
new_statements.exceptions: Some minimal pairs may be due to borrowing (e.g. /ma'ta/ 'eye' probably Tagalog); closed penults and closed antepenults never bear stress; author suggests NAlta lost inherited PPh contrastive accent and redeveloped it via borrowing, but says more data are needed; stress marking in the glossary is not consistent across all entries.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the word (roots and affixed/cliticized phonological words); data from a corpus of recordings, minimal pairs found via ELAN searches; stress shift discussed for derived words and host+enclitic phonological words.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Northern Alta [aqn], glottocode nort2875 (alternative names given: Edimala, Baler Negrito, Ditaylin Alta/Dumagat), as spoken in Diteki, Dicoliat, Dianed and Villa Aurora barangays, Aurora Province, Luzon; no dialect split is made for the stress description. Not to be confused with Southern Alta (Kabuloan, sout2905).

sources.note: Sec. 2.2.2 (p.32-34): lexical accent is phonemic (minimal pairs /'mata/ 'ripe' vs /ma'ta/ 'eye' etc.); stress may fall on open or closed ultima, open penult, or open antepenult (never a closed penult/antepenult); stressed open penults are lengthened; NAlta does not reflect PPh accent. Sec. 3.2.6 (p.67-68): certain suffixes/enclitics (-en, =i, pronouns, <in>, me-) shift stress rightward; secondary stress may remain on the original ultima. Sec. 9.1.5.2 (p.351): 'the position of the stress syllable in a word cannot be predicted', so the glossary marks stress with an acute.
